extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers in polite society (early-18th-century literate public); essayists and satirists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and responding to lampoons, satires, and public inscriptions — emphasising ethical limits, suitable targets, and tasteful expression. Focuses on the moral effects of ridicule and on appropriate form and representation (e.g., epitaphs, monuments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving secret Stabs to a Man's Reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing that more betrays a base, ungenerous Spirit, than the giving of secret Stabs to a Man's Reputation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lampoons and Satyrs, that are written with Wit and Spirit, are like poison'd Darts, which not only inflict a Wound, but make it incurable. They stir up sorrow in the heart of a private person, raise uneasiness among relations, and expose whole families to derision while the author remains unseen. Examples and historical anecdotes (Socrates/Aristophanes, Catullus/Caesar, Pasquin/Pope, Aretine) are given as illustrations of the harm such secret attacks do. Anti-pattern: anonymous, malicious lampooning of private people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper wit with virtue and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: "So pernicious a thing is Wit, when it is not tempered with Virtue and Humanity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit untethered to kindness is harmful: it can make an innocent young lady, a father of a family, a wife, or a just man the subject of ridicule and lifelong uneasiness. The essay argues it is more honourable to be a good-natured person than merely a wit. Example/fable: children pelting frogs — play for the children equates to death for the frogs (Sir Roger l'Estrange fable). Anti-pattern: cleverness pursued at the expense of others' dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making virtue or merit the subject of ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: "His Satyr will then chiefly fall upon those who ought to be the most exempt from it. Virtue, Merit, and every thing that is Praise-worthy, will be made the Subject of Ridicule and Buffoonry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vicious or ill-natured satirist tends to attack the deserving; satire should not make praise-worthy qualities objects of buffoonry. This is presented as a moral failure in the satirist and a criterion for judging whether a piece of ridicule is cruel or unjust. Anti-pattern: satirizing 'virtue' or 'merit' for cheap laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish indiscreet levity from deliberate malice
rubrics_metrics.description: The author distinguishes between heedless, inconsiderate writers who, without malice, sacrifice the reputation of friends for levity and the actively ill-natured who aim to wound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb offered: an indiscreet man (reckless levity) may be more hurtful than an ill-natured one because his levity can injure friends and acquaintances thought exempt. Writers should therefore exercise discretion: consider the consequences of raillery and avoid careless exposures of acquaintances. Example: careless lampooning that sacrifices friends' reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity/intentionally hidden authorship increases culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of the barbarous wit is ‘to stir up Sorrow... at the same time that he remains unseen and undiscovered.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous or concealed lampooning heightens its viciousness because it allows the author to inflict wounds without accountability. The text treats concealment as an aggravating feature of bad satire; historical counter-examples (severe punishments for authors when discovered) underscore risks. Best practice: avoid anonymous personal attacks; accept responsibility for satire aimed at private persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to satire with civility and reforming generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative historical responses: "When Julius Caesar was Lampoon'd by Catullus, he invited him to a Supper"; Mazarin treated Quillet with esteem and later rewarded him after passages were expunged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay presents generous, civil responses to being lampooned (invitation, admonition, reward, constructive engagement) as superior and effective: they can turn satirists into friends or reform their work. Anti-pattern: vindictive, mutilatory punishments (e.g. the Pope’s severe mutilation of a satirist) are presented as barbarous and to be condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate targets and publicness of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit guidance that satire aimed at public matters or public figures is of a different moral quality than attacks on private individuals and families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay implies a boundary: avoid exposing private misfortunes or intimate details of non-public persons. Evaluate target suitability by publicness and public consequence; private persons and domestick calamities should not be made a source of derision. Examples of harm done to private persons and families are used to illustrate the wrongness of such targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs and monuments should be elegant, just, and true to character
rubrics_metrics.description: "I could not but be very much delighted with several modern Epitaphs, which are written with great Elegance of Expression and Justness of Thought... they should be submitted to the Perusal of Men of Learning and Genius before they are put in Execution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good epitaphs honor both the living and the dead: qualities include elegance of expression, justness of thought, and accurate representation of the person's character. Anti-patterns: extravagant, falsely laudatory inscriptions ('would make the dead blush'); overly modest inscriptions in Greek/Hebrew that are unreadable; monuments whose sculpture or iconography misrepresent the subject (e.g., Cloudesly Shovel depicted as a beau rather than a rough English admiral). Recommendation: have inscriptions reviewed by learned persons; match ornamentation and symbols (rostral crowns, naval emblems) to the subject's true character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social impertinence: avoid intruding where one adds nothing to company
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters reproach 'insignificant' people who insist on appearing in better company and visiting where "they have nothing to say." One correspondent advises: "Distance and Silence are your best Recommendations" for such persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical etiquette rule: do not force oneself into company or visits if one cannot contribute to conversation or is only filling a chair. Hosts and those seeking to avoid impertinent visitors may publicly (or tactfully) set boundaries. Examples: tavern humours, unsolicited nightly visitors, and letters asking to be spared further visits.
